Executive Summary & Overview

Policy status: Active and eligiblePremiums are reported current through December 2026. Benefits may begin after Margaret satisfies the policy’s benefit trigger and elimination-period requirements.

This report consolidates the policy terms, benefit triggers, projected home-care costs, financial scenarios, and the full 90-day claim roadmap. The immediate objective is simple: open the claim promptly, create a complete evidence file, submit the claim packet by Day 30, and maintain a written record of every communication.

Critical deadlineNotify the carrier within 30 days of needing care and confirm the actual filing deadline in writing. A late or incomplete submission may delay or affect the claim.

Benefit triggers: Activities of Daily Living

Eligibility generally requires substantial assistance with at least two of six ADLs, or qualification under the policy’s severe cognitive-impairment trigger.

1 · BathingWashing the body or getting into and out of a tub or shower.
2 · DressingPutting on, taking off, or fastening clothing.
3 · EatingFeeding oneself by hand or utensil.
4 · TransferringMoving into or out of a bed, chair, or wheelchair.
5 · ToiletingUsing the toilet and managing related hygiene.
6 · ContinenceMaintaining bladder or bowel control.
Cognitive impairment triggerSevere cognitive impairment—such as dementia or Alzheimer’s disease—may qualify when ongoing supervision is necessary, even if physical ADLs remain intact. The policy’s exact wording controls.

Educational Definitions & Long-Term Impact

3% compound inflation rider
Plain languageThe benefit grows by 3% on the prior year’s amount.
Why it mattersThe projected daily benefit rises to $257.50 in Year 2 and $265.23 in Year 3.
Long-Term ImpactHigher future benefits help offset rising care costs.
Activities of Daily Living
Plain languageSix basic self-care tasks used to measure functional need.
Why it mattersNeeding substantial help with two ADLs may open access to benefits.
Long-Term ImpactConsistent medical and caregiver documentation strengthens the claim record.
Assignment of benefits
Plain languageA written authorization allowing the carrier to send eligible benefit payments directly to a provider or other designated party.
Why it mattersNot every policy or provider accepts assignment, and the client may remain responsible for unpaid balances.
Long-Term ImpactConfirm revocation rights, payment notices, reconciliation responsibilities, and who receives explanations of benefits.
Benefit period vs. lifetime maximum
Plain languageThe stated duration is three years, while the lifetime pool caps total payment.
Why it mattersThe first applicable limit reached may end benefits.
Long-Term ImpactTrack every payment against both remaining days and remaining dollars.
Benefit trigger
Plain languageThe policy condition that must be met before Margaret can qualify for covered benefits.
Why it mattersMost policies look for substantial assistance with at least two Activities of Daily Living or severe cognitive impairment, but the policy's exact wording controls.
Long-Term ImpactEarly clinical documentation can reduce delays and create a clearer record if the carrier requests more evidence.

LTC STRATEGY REPORT
04

Educational Definitions & Long-Term Impact — Continued

C.N.A. caregiver requirement
Plain languageA policy rule that may require care to be provided by a currently certified nursing assistant or another specifically qualified provider.
Why it mattersAppropriate care can still be denied reimbursement if the caregiver does not meet the policy’s credential standard.
Long-Term ImpactVerify credentials before service begins and retain current certification or agency records in the claim file.
Calendar-day vs. service-day elimination period
Plain languageCalendar days may pass continuously after eligibility begins; service days generally count only on days qualifying care is received.
Why it mattersA 90-day waiting period can take much longer than 90 calendar days when only covered service days count.
Long-Term ImpactConfirm the counting method in writing before setting aside funds for the waiting period.
Care logs or logsheets
Plain languageVisit-by-visit records showing service dates, times, tasks, observations, signatures, and sometimes ADL assistance.
Why it mattersThe carrier may use logsheets to match invoices with covered services and the approved plan of care.
Long-Term ImpactIncomplete or inconsistent logs can delay payment; review them before each submission.
Case manager
Plain languageA carrier representative or clinical professional who coordinates claim review, care authorization, and ongoing monitoring.
Why it mattersThe case manager may request records, arrange assessments, explain next steps, or review changes in care needs.
Long-Term ImpactRecord the case manager’s full contact information and confirm material instructions in writing.
Cognitive impairment
Plain languageA severe loss of cognitive ability that requires supervision for safety.
Why it mattersIt may trigger benefits without two physical ADL limitations.
Long-Term ImpactThe policy can address both physical decline and cognitive care needs.

Educational Definitions & Helpful Claim Information

Current remaining benefit balance
Plain languageThe carrier’s current accounting of unused covered dollars and, when applicable, remaining covered days.
Why it mattersThe original lifetime maximum is not necessarily the amount still available after prior claims or adjustments.
Long-Term ImpactRequest an updated written balance regularly and investigate discrepancies before they compound.
Daily maximum benefit
Plain languageThe most the policy may pay for eligible covered services received on one day.
Why it mattersExpenses above the daily cap are generally the client's responsibility, even when the service itself is covered.
Long-Term ImpactCompare each day’s eligible charges with the cap and track whether unused amounts remain in the benefit pool.
Eligible provider
Plain languageA caregiver, agency, or facility that satisfies the policy's licensing, certification, and relationship rules.
Why it mattersCare can be medically appropriate yet still be ineligible if the provider does not meet the policy definition.
Long-Term ImpactObtain written carrier confirmation before care starts or before changing agencies or caregivers.
Elimination period
Plain languageThe waiting period Margaret must satisfy before reimbursement begins.
Why it mattersAt $250 per day, 90 days creates a $22,500 planning obligation.
Long-Term ImpactFunding this gap prevents disruption while the claim is reviewed.
Guaranteed renewable
Plain languageThe insurer generally cannot cancel the policy because Margaret's health changes, as long as required premiums are paid.
Why it mattersGuaranteed renewable does not necessarily mean premiums can never increase for an approved class of policyholders.
Long-Term ImpactReview every rate notice promptly and compare any reduced-benefit options before making an irreversible change.

04

Educational Definitions & Policy Protections

Indemnity or cash benefit
Plain languageThe policy may pay a fixed eligible amount after qualification, rather than matching each dollar of care expense.
Why it mattersPayment rules, documentation requirements, and tax reporting may differ from a reimbursement policy.
Long-Term ImpactVerify the payment method before building the care budget or assuming unused daily benefits remain available.
Lifetime maximum benefit
Plain languageThe maximum total dollars the policy can pay over its life, subject to riders and policy provisions.
Why it mattersThe lifetime pool may be exhausted before the stated benefit period ends when care costs are high.
Long-Term ImpactReconcile every payment against the carrier’s official benefit ledger and projected future care needs.
Minimum ADL requirement
Plain languageThe minimum number of Activities of Daily Living for which the insured must need the policy-defined level of assistance.
Why it mattersThe number alone is not enough; the type and duration of assistance must match the policy wording.
Long-Term ImpactKeep physician, assessment, plan-of-care, and caregiver documentation consistent across every ADL.
Monthly maximum benefit
Plain languageA separate limit on what the policy may pay during a calendar month or benefit month.
Why it mattersA monthly cap may restrict payment even when no individual service day exceeds the daily maximum.
Long-Term ImpactConfirm the month definition, proration rules, and treatment of months with 28, 30, or 31 days.
Nonforfeiture benefit
Plain languageA protection that may preserve reduced paid-up benefits if the policy lapses after required conditions are met.
Why it mattersIt is not the same as a refund and may provide only a limited future benefit.
Long-Term ImpactBefore reducing or stopping premiums, request the exact lapse and nonforfeiture consequences in writing.

04

Educational Definitions & Claim Review

Payment cycle to the client
Plain languageThe carrier’s recurring process for receiving records, reviewing eligible charges, and issuing benefit payments.
Why it mattersMonthly, biweekly, or other cycles affect cash flow and how quickly missing documentation must be corrected.
Long-Term ImpactMaintain enough liquidity to cover care while invoices are under review or payment is pending.
Plan of care and care coordinator
Plain languageA written care plan identifies needs, services, frequency, and goals; a care coordinator may help assess and organize approved care.
Why it mattersThe carrier may require a plan prescribed or approved by an authorized health-care professional.
Long-Term ImpactUpdate the plan when needs change so service records continue to match the approved level of care.
Pre-claim vs. claim number
Plain languageA pre-claim number tracks the evaluation; a permanent claim number follows approval.
Why it mattersBoth connect correspondence and documents to the correct case.
Long-Term ImpactPut the assigned number on every submission and care invoice.
Proof of loss, claim decision, and appeal
Plain languageProof of loss is the documentation supporting a claim; the decision explains approval, limitation, or denial; an appeal requests reconsideration.
Why it mattersPolicies and carrier notices may impose submission, response, and appeal deadlines.
Long-Term ImpactKeep complete copies, delivery confirmation, decision letters, call notes, and appeal materials in one claim file.
Reimbursement benefit
Plain languageThe carrier pays eligible documented expenses, usually up to the policy's daily or monthly maximum.
Why it mattersInvoices, service dates, proof of payment, and provider credentials may be required before payment is released.
Long-Term ImpactStrong monthly recordkeeping helps prevent missed reimbursements and makes the remaining benefit balance easier to track.

LTC STRATEGY REPORT
04

Educational Definitions & Documentation

Restoration of benefits
Plain languageA rider or provision that may restore some used benefits after recovery and a required claim-free period.
Why it mattersNot every policy includes restoration, and qualifying conditions can be strict.
Long-Term ImpactIf included, restoration can preserve protection for a later, separate episode of care.
Tax-qualified long-term care policy
Plain languageA contract designed to meet federal requirements under Internal Revenue Code Section 7702B.
Why it mattersQualified benefits are generally treated favorably for federal income-tax purposes, subject to applicable limits and individual circumstances.
Long-Term ImpactRetain Form 1099-LTC and consult a qualified tax professional before treating benefits or premiums on a tax return.
Third-party assessment
Plain languageAn independent functional or clinical assessment requested by the carrier, often performed by a nurse or contracted assessor.
Why it mattersThe assessment may influence whether benefit triggers are satisfied and what services are approved.
Long-Term ImpactPrepare accurate medication, diagnosis, ADL, cognition, safety, and care-history information before the visit.
Waiver of premium
Plain languageA policy provision that may suspend premium payments after specified claim conditions are met.
Why it mattersThe waiver may begin only after benefit eligibility, the elimination period, or another policy milestone.
Long-Term ImpactDo not stop paying premiums until the carrier confirms the waiver's effective date in writing.
Worksheet reviewer and verification date
Plain languageThe printed name of the person who reviewed the worksheet and the date that review occurred.
Why it mattersIt shows who recorded the information and when the carrier details and benefit fields were last checked.
Long-Term ImpactRe-date and re-verify the worksheet after claim decisions, benefit changes, new care needs, or carrier instructions.

Home Care Cost Analysis

How home care works with an LTC policy

Home care brings trained support into Margaret’s home for daily routines, personal care, companionship, safety oversight, and other approved needs. The agency delivers and documents the care; the insurer decides whether the policy’s trigger, provider rules, service definitions, daily maximum, and elimination period have been satisfied. Visiting Angels can help coordinate the practical side, but only the carrier can approve and pay a claim.

Action Checklist by Phase

  • Days 1–7
    Immediate    Collect the policy, 12 months of medical records, physician notes, test results, medication list, current care-needs summary, provider information, and identification. Create one chronological claim folder and schedule the primary-care appointment.
  • Days 8–15
    Carrier    Call Genworth. Request the claim packet, pre-claim number, assigned case manager, required-document list, benefit-trigger language, provider rules, and written confirmation of deadlines. Log the date, time, representative, and reference number.
  • Days 16–30
    Forms    Complete the Claimant Statement. Ask the physician to complete the Attending Physician Statement with functional details. Review all signatures and dates, copy the entire packet, transmit securely, and obtain proof of receipt.
  • Days 31–45
    Medical review    Respond rapidly to requests for additional records. Keep the case manager updated, document every exchange, reconcile inconsistent ADL descriptions, and prepare Margaret and the caregiver for the functional assessment.
  • Days 46–60
    Assessment    Schedule the in-home or functional assessment. Keep care records available, describe limitations accurately without minimizing them, invite a knowledgeable caregiver or family member, and document the assessment date and outcome.
  • Days 61–75
    Approval    Review the decision letter and permanent claim number. Compare the approved benefit, elimination-period determination, provider eligibility, reimbursement method, and effective date against the policy. Question discrepancies in writing.
  • Days 76–90
    Activation    Finalize the care schedule, provider agreement, invoicing details, direct-pay or reimbursement setup, and monthly care-log process. Confirm when the first eligible invoice may be submitted.
  • Ongoing
    Monthly    Submit complete invoices and care logs; track service dates, daily benefit use, remaining pool, correspondence, and changes in condition. Retain copies and review the policy and plan of care annually.

Estimates and privacy. Costs, timelines, care needs, inflation, rates, and projected savings may change. Transmit medical and policy records securely, verify the recipient, retain confirmation, and do not send a full Social Security number through unsecured channels.
